event: Elsie wakes at dawn to the grey glove on the sill by Moonpenny, and says good morning to both.
She waters the crate, Mrs Pennywhistle to Doris, and tells Moonpenny she's taking Noor cakes.
She dresses, re-knots the snapped bootlace tighter, and tucks Noor's parcel into her satchel.
She packs the second glove too, still only a cuff on its needles.
Downstairs Agnes is shaking out a flour sack and frowning at the grit in the bottom of it.
Agnes says Hobb Mill's flour has come short and gritty all month, and Bess Hobb is behind.
Agnes says a girl with long braids stood at the window last night, a good while, and didn't knock.
Elsie claps her hands and says she came, and her eyes fill, and Agnes hands her a cloth.
Elsie leaves the honey cakes in the window another day, in case, and Agnes lets her.
Tamsin knocks at the shop door early, Margery on her shoulder, yawning, curls still damp.
Elsie gives her a honey cake off the plate; Tamsin eats it in two bites and licks her thumb.
Elsie tells Tamsin about the girl with braids; Tamsin says Amara will come when she's brave enough.
They walk along Thimble Canal toward Brightwater Square in the mist coming off the water.
At a coffee stall on the square Elsie buys a cup of black coffee, strong, nothing in it: two pips.
Tamsin asks who drinks that muck; Elsie says it's in her book, under the raincloud.
Tilly is sitting on the guild steps with a fat book of grave things open on her knees.
Tilly says she read till two and knows nine ways to stop a wight, and is very sorry for the wight.
Inside, Cora stands by the clerk's desk, ledger under her arm; the harebell is gone from her coat.
Elsie asks after it; Cora says it wilted, so she pressed it, then looks sorry she said so.
Elsie asks if Cora slept; Cora says yes, and Elsie sees the grey under her eyes and doubts it.
Cora says the guildmaster read the barrow report, and asked nothing about the empty name.
Noor sits alone in her ring of empty tables, a cup in her gloved hand, eyes on the door.
Elsie crosses the ring with the coffee, catches her toe on nothing, and pitches forward.
Tamsin's hand shoots past her and takes the cup out of the air; not a drop goes over.
Elsie sets the coffee in front of Noor: black, strong, nothing in it, like her book says.
Noor looks at the cup a long time, then wraps both gloved hands round it and drinks.
Elsie tests the chair with both hands before sitting; it holds, and she beams.
She sets the brown parcel by the cup; Noor reads her own name on it, and the little raincloud.
Noor asks what it is; Elsie says honey cakes, she made them, the crust is a baker's trick.
Noor doesn't open it; she slips it inside her coat, against her chest, and buttons the coat over it.
Elsie's flower clip springs out of her hair and lands in Noor's lap.
Noor picks it up in two gloved fingers and holds it out; Elsie asks her to put it back in, please.
Noor leans across and clips it in above Elsie's ear, gloved fingers slow in her hair.
Noor's breath is close and uneven, and her fingers stay at Elsie's temple a moment too long.
She sits back fast, eyes on her cup, and her ears have gone pink under the black hair.
Elsie says she can't sit long today: there's a notice. So she brought lunch to Noor instead.
Noor says, dryly, that this is cheating; Elsie says it isn't, she'll be back tomorrow.
Cora comes into the ring and stops at the table; Noor looks up and says: Vane.
Cora says: Haddad. Elsie asks, delighted, if they know each other.
Noor says Cora has the rooms over hers on Wick Lane; they pass on the stair and have never spoken.
Noor adds that Cora walks the floor at night, back and forth, and came in past eleven last night.
Cora goes red to the collar; Elsie says that's because Cora never sleeps, and pats her arm.
Tamsin, at the board, calls out the E-rank notice: a boggart fouling the wheel at Hobb Mill.
Elsie says Hobb Mill grinds Agnes's flour, so that settles it; Tilly sighs: not a grave thing.
Noor says boggarts throw stones, and tells Elsie, not quite lightly, to keep her head down.
At the clerk's desk Tamsin signs the party for the notice: nine lanterns; Cora writes in her ledger.
Elsie waves to Noor from the door; Noor lifts her hand higher than yesterday.
They go out by the south gate onto the river road beside the Wend.
Elsie knits the second glove as she walks; the cuff grows, two plain, two purl.
Cora walks at her side watching the needles, and asks nothing this time.
Cora says a boggart is a house-spirit, and the guild's books class it as a pest to be removed.
Elsie says the notice says the wheel, not the boggart, and Cora writes that down.
They reach Hobb Mill: tall stone, a great wooden wheel standing still, a willow, a thatched cottage.
Bess Hobb, stout, floury, meets them with her two grown daughters and says the race is choked again.
The wheel is jammed with river weed and stones packed into the paddles, tight as mortar.
Tamsin wades into the race to her waist and hauls stones out, swearing at each one cheerfully.
Tilly passes weed up the bank in armfuls; Elsie, on the sluice, works the slimy stones loose.
Cora, coat off and sleeves rolled, takes the stones from Elsie's hands one by one and stacks them.
Elsie's hands slip, and Cora catches her wrist and holds it until she has her footing.
By three the wheel turns again, and Bess says it'll be choked by morning, it always is.
The younger daughter says it started the week after Gran died, and Bess tells her to hush.
Elsie asks what Gran used to do of an evening; the daughter says she left cream on the back step.
Bess says that was Mam's nonsense; Elsie sees her face and says it doesn't sound like nonsense.
Bess sits down on the mill step and cries, once, hard, and Elsie sits by her and holds her hand.
Elsie says the boggart misses Gran too, and might only want thanking; Bess says she'll try it.
Supper in the cottage is bread of the mill's own flour and pea soup, and Bess won't take a pip.
At dusk Bess sets a bowl of cream on the back step by the wheel, and they wait under the willow.
A stone comes out of the dark and cracks against the step; then another, close by Elsie's knee.
Tamsin half rises; Elsie puts out a hand and says stay, and Cora shutters her lantern to a thread.
A knee-high hairy thing creeps up the bank to the bowl, eyes like wet pebbles, and drinks.
Bess, voice cracking, thanks it for keeping the stones out of the race all those years, as Mam did.
Elsie says thank you too, very softly, for the wheel and for the flour in her honey cakes.
The boggart looks at them over the bowl, and between one blink and the next it is gone.
Cora opens her ledger by the thread of lamplight and writes: skills used, none.
Bess gives them the loft over the flour store, sacks for beds and two blankets for four.
Tamsin flops on the sacks by the ladder and is snoring like a little kettle in a minute.
Tilly takes one blanket with Elsie and curls against her back, her nose in Elsie's hair.
Cora sits against the wall to watch; Elsie says not two nights running, and lifts the blanket.
Cora lies down at Elsie's front, very straight, in her shirtsleeves, not quite touching.
Elsie finds Cora's hands cold again and takes them between hers to warm them.
She lays her palm flat to Cora's; Cora's fingers are longer by a whole knuckle, and Elsie is glad.
Under Elsie's thumb Cora's pulse is running fast; Elsie thinks she's still cold, and holds on.
Cora whispers Fairweather and nothing after it, and Elsie whispers back goodnight, Cora.
Out in the dark the wheel turns and turns, clear, and Elsie falls asleep to it.
